lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, Traveling is the best way to learn! Skye flies with us part of the way, then waves goodbye. We walk with Ms. Emma into a town called Willowford. Look! There's a big old building with a round green roof and wide stone steps. It's the Hall of Wisdom! Inside, there is a round meeting hall with seats in a circle. A barn owl with round glasses flies down, holding a small wooden bell. Ding! She says, Welcome! I'm Olive, the chairperson of the Children's Council. Every voice matters! Birimo whispers, What is a council? Ms. Emma says, It's a group that meets to share ideas and decide things together. Olive says, Children from many places meet here to talk. Say it with me. Children from many places meet here to talk. Wonderful! In the center, an old tree grows indoors with six empty branches. Olive says, This is the Tree of Voices. When children share ideas kindly and listen well, a golden leaf grows. Let's read the sign by the door. "Welcome to the Hall of Wisdom! Here, children from many places meet to talk about things that matter to them. At the Children's Council, everyone can speak, and everyone listens. You may agree, or you may disagree, but please be kind. Raise your hand when you want to speak, and wait for your turn. Remember, good listeners make good speakers. Every voice matters!" When do you raise your hand? When you want to speak. Who makes a good speaker? A good listener. Then we meet three new friends. Leo is from a mountain town and loves soccer. Amara is from a seaside village and loves animals. Priya is from a big city and loves books. Now, phonics. Ity makes a noun. Equal becomes equality. Diverse, drop the e, becomes diversity. Curious changes ous to os: curiosity. Say the part before ity strongly. e-QUAL-i-ty, di-VER-si-ty, cu-ri-OS-i-ty. Next time, the council talks about school uniforms!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, Children from many places meet here to talk. This morning, twenty council children sit in the big circle. We sit with Ms. Emma, and Birimo is so excited that he can't stop wiggling. Olive rings her little wooden bell. Ding! She says, Good morning, everyone! Here is our first question. Should students wear uniforms? Say it with me. Should students wear uniforms? Great! Olive says, There is no wrong answer. Let's listen to both sides. Leo raises his hand first. Then Priya raises her hand. Let's read what they said. "Leo says: At my school, we all wear uniforms. I think uniforms are good because everyone looks the same, so nobody feels bad about their clothes. Getting ready in the morning is quick, too. Priya says: My school doesn't have uniforms. I think choosing our own clothes is better because it shows our personality and creativity. Also, uniforms can cost a lot, and they are not always comfortable." Why does Leo like uniforms? Because nobody feels bad about their clothes, and the mornings are quick. What can our clothes show, according to Priya? Our personality. Now, here is a fun question. Leo's school has uniforms. Is that a fact or an opinion? It's a fact, because we can check it. Uniforms are better than our own clothes. Is that a fact or an opinion? It's an opinion, because people think differently. Amara says, I see your point, Leo, but I like choosing my own clothes. Leo smiles and says, That's fine! We can think differently and still be friends. Olive says, Thank you both. You disagreed so politely! Now, phonics. Today's words end in ity, too. Personal becomes personality. Creative, drop the e, becomes creativity. Similar becomes similarity. Say the part before ity strongly. per-son-AL-i-ty, cre-a-TIV-i-ty, sim-i-LAR-i-ty. Next time, Amara asks the council a new question: should we have longer breaks?

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, Should students wear uniforms? Today, Olive rings her bell, and Amara raises her hand. She says, At my school, break time is only ten minutes. That's not enough time to go outside and come back! Olive says, Thank you, Amara. Who has an opinion? Remember to give a reason. Haru raises his hand and says, I think we should have longer breaks because we need time to relax. Say it with me. I think we should have longer breaks because we need time to relax. Excellent! An opinion is stronger with a reason and an example. Haru adds, For example, we can play outside and talk with our friends. Then Priya says, I partly agree. But then school will finish later. Both ideas are fair. Olive gives everyone a short article from the Hall's newsletter. Let's read the article. "Do children need longer breaks? Some people say yes. After a good break, many children can concentrate better in class. Break time is also an important activity, because children make friends, solve small problems, and move their bodies. Other people worry about longer breaks. If breaks are longer, the school day may finish later, or there may be less time for lessons. One possibility is to keep the same timetable but add one long break at lunchtime." Why can children concentrate better? Because they had a good break. What is one possibility? One long break at lunchtime. Leo says, I like that idea. Kiko says, Me, too, but let's ask the teachers what they think. Olive smiles and says, Good listeners make good speakers! Now, phonics. Active, drop the e, add ity. Activity. Able changes ble to bil. Ability. Possible changes ble to bil, too. Possibility. Say the part before ity strongly. ac-TIV-i-ty, a-BIL-i-ty, pos-si-BIL-i-ty. Next time, Priya brings the results of a survey about school rules!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, I think we should have longer breaks because we need time to relax. Today, Priya stands in the middle of the circle with a big sheet of paper. She did a survey! She asked all twenty council children five questions about school rules. Of course, the survey has no names, so nobody had to share private information. Priya says, Here are the results. Most students want to choose their own seats. Say it with me. Most students want to choose their own seats. Great! Most means more than half. When we talk about numbers, we can also say, Fifteen out of twenty. Let's read Priya's survey results. "School Rules Survey. Twenty council children answered. Fifteen out of twenty want to choose their own seats in class. Twelve want longer breaks. Eight think students should wear uniforms, and twelve do not. Seventeen think phones should stay in our bags during lessons. Only a few students, just two, want more homework! Thank you for answering. Your answers help us understand each other." How many children want to choose their own seats? Fifteen out of twenty. How many want more homework? Only two. Leo laughs and says, I'm one of the two! I like homework because it helps me remember. Priya says, That's a fact I didn't know about you! Then Kiko raises her hand. She says, I partly agree with choosing seats, but some people might feel left out. Olive rings her bell gently. She says, That's an important point, Kiko. Rules should be fair for everyone. Now, phonics. Look at the word before ity. Major becomes majority. The majority means more than half. Popular becomes popularity. Responsible changes ble to bil and becomes responsibility. Say the part before ity strongly. ma-JOR-i-ty, pop-u-LAR-i-ty, re-spon-si-BIL-i-ty. Next time, we look at both sides of the uniform question again, and something golden may happen!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, Most students want to choose their own seats. Today is our big school rules discussion. Olive rings her bell and says, Let's think about uniforms one more time. This time, let's look at both sides together. Ms. Emma holds out her right hand and says, On the one hand（いっぽうでは）, uniforms save time. Then she holds out her left hand and says, On the other hand, students can't choose their clothes. Say it with me. On the one hand, uniforms save time. On the other hand, students can't choose their clothes. Fantastic! This is a great way to show two points of view. Every idea has advantages and disadvantages. Birimo asks, What do you mean by save time? Leo answers, I mean we don't have to choose clothes every morning. Then Priya writes a summary on the big board. Let's read the summary. "Our School Rules Discussion. Uniforms: On the one hand, they save time, and everyone looks equal. On the other hand, students can't choose their clothes, and uniforms can cost a lot. Longer breaks: On the one hand, they help us relax and concentrate. On the other hand, school may finish later. Choosing seats: Most students like it, but nobody should feel left out. Thank you for listening to each other!" What is one disadvantage of uniforms? They can cost a lot. What is one advantage of longer breaks? They help us relax. Olive looks around the circle. She says, You shared your ideas kindly, and you listened so well. lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, On the one hand, uniforms save time. On the other hand, students can't choose their clothes. The first golden leaf is still shining on the Tree of Voices. Today, Olive rings her bell and says, Our next topic is fairness. Amara raises her hand. She looks a little sad. She says, At my school, there is only one soccer ball. Some older students take it every day, and the younger children just watch. Kiko frowns and says, It's not fair if only some people can play. Say it with me. It's not fair if only some people can play. Good! Amara wrote a short story about it for the council. Let's read Amara's story. "Every day at break time, my friend Nina runs to the field with a big smile. But every day, the same older students are already there with the ball. They play well, and they have a lot of fun. Nina waits by the fence and hopes they will ask her to join. They never do. Nina thinks, Is that fair? I don't think so. But maybe they don't know that I want to play, too." Where does Nina wait? By the fence. What does Nina think the older students don't know? That she wants to play, too. Leo says, I see your point, but the older students got there first. Priya says, I partly agree, Leo. But the ball belongs to the whole school. Olive says, Thank you both. It's important to understand everyone, even the older students. Maybe nobody told them how Nina feels. Now, phonics. Inter means between, or with each other. Co means together. International means between nations, like our council. Interview means two people see each other and talk. Cooperate means work together. Next time, the council will think of ways for everyone to join in!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, It's not fair if only some people can play. Today, Olive rings her bell and says, Let's help Nina and the younger children. How can we make break time fair? Leo stands up. He says, I love soccer, and I want everyone to love it, too. Everyone should have a chance to try. Say it with me. Everyone should have a chance to try. Super! Riko asks, How about taking turns? Priya says, That's a good idea. Haru adds, Why don't we make mixed teams? Then big kids and small kids can play together. Leo wrote a plan for the council. Let's read Leo's plan. "The Break Time Ball Plan. Everyone should have a chance to try. Monday and Wednesday: younger students use the ball. Tuesday and Thursday: older students use the ball. Friday: Mixed Team Day! We make teams with big and small players, so every team is fair. Older students can help younger players and teach them new tricks. Write your name on the sign-up sheet by the door. Let's play together!" Who uses the ball on Monday? The younger students. What happens on Friday? We make mixed teams. Amara says, I like Mixed Team Day because the older and younger kids can interact and become friends. But Kiko says, I partly agree. A sign-up sheet might take a long time every day. Leo says, That's a good point. Maybe one helper can write the names each morning. Olive smiles. She says, Look how well you work together, like a pilot and a copilot! Now, phonics. Inter means between, or with each other. Interact means do things with each other. An intersection is the place between roads, where they cross. Co means together. A copilot flies a plane together with the pilot. Next time, we will learn what to do when someone is unkind to a friend.

lines.speaker: Ms. Emma
lines.en: How can we make break time fair for Nina and her friends?
lines.ja: ニーナや その 友だちに とって 休み時間を 公平に するには どう したら いいかしら？

lines.speaker: Birimo
lines.en: I'm playing Leo! I love soccer. Everyone should have a chance to try.
lines.ja: ぼく、レオの やく！ サッカーが 大すき。みんなに やって みる チャンスが ある べきだよ。

lines.speaker: Riko
lines.en: How about taking turns? Younger kids on Monday, older kids on Tuesday.
lines.ja: じゅんばんに したら どう？ 月曜日は 小さい 子、火曜日は 上の 子。

lines.speaker: Haru
lines.en: That's a good idea. Why don't we make mixed teams, too? Big and small kids can play together.
lines.ja: それは いい アイデアだね。まぜた チームも つくらない？ 大きい 子と 小さい 子が いっしょに あそべるよ。

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, Everyone should have a chance to try. Today, Olive brings a picture book from the Hall's library. She says, Sometimes we see someone being unkind. What can we do? Let's think about it together. First, Ms. Emma tells us three important things. Never fight, and never laugh along. Stand up for your friend with calm, kind words. And always tell a teacher or another adult right away. You can say, Stop it. That's not kind. Say it with me. Stop it. That's not kind. Well done! Say it calmly, not angrily. Let's read the story. "Tom loves drawing. One day, Mia picks up his picture and laughs. Your dog looks like a potato, she says, and she teases him in front of everyone. Tom looks down. His friend Sam stands up and says calmly, Stop it. That's not kind. Then Sam stands next to Tom and asks, Are you OK? I'll stay with you. Together, they tell their teacher right away. The next day, Mia comes to Tom and says, I'm sorry. I was wrong. Tom accepts her apology, and they draw a dog together." What does Sam say to Mia? Stop it. That's not kind. What does Mia do the next day? She says sorry. Priya says, I think telling a teacher is the most important part because adults can help. Amara says, I partly agree. Staying with Tom is important, too, because then he doesn't feel scared. Leo says, I like the ending. People can change. Olive nods and says, Different people can coexist when we are kind to each other. Now, phonics. Inter means between, or with each other. The internet is networks connected with each other. Co means together. A coworker works together with you. Coexist means live together. Next time, we will learn how to invite someone to join us at break time!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, Stop it. That's not kind. Today, there is a short break between council meetings. Olive calls it an intermission. We go out to the Hall's garden with Ms. Emma and play a ball game with Leo and Amara. Then Kiko sees a new council child named Ken. He is sitting by himself on a bench, looking at a book. Kiko walks over with a smile. She says, Hi, Ken. Do you want to join us? Say it with me. Do you want to join us? Lovely! Ken looks up and says, Sure! Thank you for asking. He kicks the ball, and everyone cheers. Later, Amara shows us a poster she made with Priya. Let's read the poster. "How to Include Everyone. Look around at break time. Is anyone sitting by themselves? Walk over, smile, and say, Do you want to join us? Use their name if you know it. Some people may want quiet time, and that is OK, too. You can say, Maybe next time! Nobody should feel left out. A small question can make a big friend." What can you say to invite someone? Do you want to join us? What if someone wants quiet time? That's OK. Say, Maybe next time. Haru says, I think we should always invite people because nobody likes to feel left out. Riko says, I partly agree. But some people really like reading quietly, so we should ask first and listen to the answer. Ken laughs. He says, Today I wanted to play. But tomorrow, I might want to finish my book! Amara and Priya are the coauthors of the poster, because they wrote it together. Now, phonics. Inter means between. An intermission is a break between parts of a show. Co means together. A coauthor writes a book together with someone. A costar is a star of a movie together with another star. Next time, we will start a Kindness Campaign!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, Do you want to join us? Today is a special day. Olive rings her bell and says, This week, we talked about fairness and kindness. Now, let's share what we learned with the whole Hall. It's time for our Kindness Campaign! We work in groups with Leo, Amara, Priya, and Ken. We cooperate, and everyone uses their own ability. Amara draws pictures, Priya checks the spelling, and Leo thinks of the slogan. Haru stands up with the poster and says, Let's make our school a kind place. Say it with me. Let's make our school a kind place. Beautiful! Then the four friends give their presentation. Let's read the poster. "Kindness Campaign. Let's make our school a kind place! First, say hello to everyone, even people you don't know yet. Second, take turns and share, so everyone has a fair chance. Finally, invite people to play, and listen if they want quiet time. If you see someone being unkind, say calmly, Stop it, and tell a teacher right away. Kind words make a happy school!" What is the second idea? Take turns and share. What should you do if you see someone being unkind? Say, Stop it, and tell a teacher. At the end, Kiko says, Thank you for listening. Do you have any questions? Priya asks, Which idea is the most important? Kiko says, I think inviting people is the most important because nobody feels left out. Haru says, I partly agree, but saying hello is the easiest way to start. Olive says, You listened to each other so well. Then the Tree of Voices shines again, and a second golden leaf grows! Now, phonics. Let's review. International. Inter means between, so it means between nations. Cooperate. Co means together, so it means work together. Ability. Able changes ble to bil and adds ity. a-BIL-i-ty. Next time, Olive will tell us about something very important that many countries agreed on.

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, Let's make our school a kind place. Our Kindness Campaign was a big success, and today the Children's Council meets again. Olive rings her little wooden bell. Ding! She says, Every voice matters! Today, let's talk about something very important: children's rights. A right is something that every child should have, wherever they live. A long time ago, in 1989, many countries agreed on a list of children's rights. For example, children have the right to go to school. They have the right to play and rest. Leo grins and says, So soccer is a right! Everyone laughs, even Olive. Children have the right to learn and play. Say it with me. Children have the right to learn and play. Great! Olive points to a big poster on the wall. Let's read the poster. "Every child has rights. You have the right to learn, so you can go to school and ask questions. You have the right to play and rest, because your body and mind need time to grow. You have the right to be safe and healthy. You have the right to say what you think and be listened to. These rights are for every child, everywhere. And with rights come responsibilities, too." Why do children need to play and rest? Because their body and mind need time to grow. Who are these rights for? Every child, everywhere. Priya raises her hand and asks, What do you mean by responsibilities? Olive smiles. A responsibility is something you should do, like listening to others. Now, phonics. When we compare two things or correct someone, we say the new word strongly. Do you like that one? No, I like THIS one. Did you say Tuesday? No, I said THURSDAY. Should we meet at three? No, let's meet at FOUR. Is the library on the left? No, it's on the RIGHT. Next time, Amara will tell us all about her dog and her cat!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, Children have the right to learn and play. Today, Amara brings her drawing book to the Children's Council. She loves animals, and she has drawn her two pets. Biscuit is a fluffy brown dog with floppy ears, and Pepper is a sleepy gray cat. Amara says, I love them so much, but having pets is not only fun. It's also a big job. Olive nods. That's a responsibility! When we have pets, we have to feed them, give them water, and keep them healthy. We are responsible for taking care of our pets. Say it with me. We are responsible for taking care of our pets. Excellent! Amara shows us the pet care chart from her kitchen wall. Let's read the chart. "Biscuit and Pepper's Care Chart. Morning: Amara walks Biscuit with Dad and fills both water bowls. Evening: Amara feeds Pepper, and her brother feeds Biscuit. Every Saturday: we brush Biscuit's fur and clean Pepper's bed. When a pet looks sick, we tell an adult, and we visit the vet together. Pets can't talk, so we watch them carefully. A happy pet needs food, water, exercise, and lots of love." Who feeds Pepper? Amara does. What do they do when a pet looks sick? They tell an adult and visit the vet together. Then Leo asks a question. Should children walk the dog every day? Haru thinks so, because dogs need exercise. Riko partly agrees. She says an adult should come, too, because the roads can be busy. Now, phonics. Remember, when we correct someone, the new word is strong. Do you feed the cat? No, I feed the DOG. Does Haru feed the fish? No, KIKO feeds the fish. Do you walk the dog at night? No, I walk him in the MORNING. Is the bowl empty? No, the bowl is FULL. Next time, let's talk about our jobs at home!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, We are responsible for taking care of our pets. Today, Olive asks the council a new question. What jobs do you do at home? These jobs are called chores. Leo says, I take out the trash bags. Amara says, I fold the laundry. Kiko says, I set the table, and I'm responsible for washing the dishes. Say it with me. I'm responsible for washing the dishes. Super! Priya laughs and says, In my family, we have a chore chart, so everyone knows their job. She shows us a photo of it. Let's read Priya's chore chart. "The Family Team Chart. Mom cooks dinner on weekdays, and Dad cooks on weekends. Priya is responsible for setting the table and feeding the fish. Her little brother puts the spoons away. Priya's big sister helps Mom cook, and Grandpa waters the plants. Every Saturday morning, we clean the house together and play music. When everyone helps a little, nobody is too tired, and we have more time for games." Who cooks dinner on weekends? Dad does. When does the family clean the house? Every Saturday morning. Then Olive asks, Should children help at home every day? Riko says yes, because a family is a team. Haru partly agrees. He thinks small jobs are enough on busy school days, because children also need time for homework and play. Olive rings her bell. Ding! Both of you gave good reasons! Now, phonics. Let's practice the strong new word again. Do you wash the dishes? No, I DRY the dishes. Does your brother cook? No, my SISTER cooks. Do you clean on Sunday? No, we clean on SATURDAY. Are you making lunch? No, I'm making DINNER. Next time, we will think about what children can do for Willowford, our community!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, I'm responsible for washing the dishes. We help our families at home. But what about our town? Today, Olive takes us to the big window of the Hall of Wisdom. We can see all of Willowford: little red roofs, a library with a clock, and the green trees of Willowford Park. Olive says, This town is a community. A community is all the people who live and work in a place. What can children do for our community? Say it with me. What can children do for our community? Wonderful! Leo says, We can say hello to our neighbors. It's easy, and it makes people smile. Priya says, We can help at the library and put the books back on the shelves. Then Ms. Emma finds a notice on the board by the door. Let's read the notice. "Willowford Park Clean-Up Day. Join us on Saturday afternoon from one to three! Bring a hat and a water bottle. We will give you gloves, tongs, and bags. Children must come with an adult. Last spring, our volunteers picked up forty bags of litter and planted sunflowers near the pond. Let's make our park clean and beautiful again. Thank you, Willowford!" When is the clean-up? On Saturday afternoon, from one to three. What did the volunteers plant last spring? Sunflowers. Kiko says, Why don't we join the clean-up? Ms. Emma says, Good idea, but we'll all go together with the adults. Now, phonics. Listen to the strong new words. Did you plant roses? No, we planted SUNFLOWERS. Is the event on Saturday morning? No, it's on Saturday AFTERNOON. Do you want the big poster? No, I want the SMALL poster. Is the station near the school? No, it's near the LIBRARY. Next time, we will give a talk about rights and responsibilities!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, What can children do for our community? On Saturday afternoon, we cleaned Willowford Park with Ms. Emma and the other adults, and we said hello to so many neighbors. Today is a special day. Each group will give a short talk about rights and responsibilities. Priya interviews Leo about safety at school. Amara talks about her pets. Then it's our turn. Riko stands up and says, I'd like to talk about rights and responsibilities. Olive says, Go ahead. We're listening. Riko's big idea is this. We have the right to speak, and we should listen to others. Say it with me. We have the right to speak, and we should listen to others. Beautiful! Let's read Riko's speech. "Hello, everyone. Children have many rights. We have the right to learn, so we should try our best at school. We have the right to play, so we should share the ball and take turns. We have the right to be safe, so we should help keep our town clean and safe. And we have the right to speak, and we should listen to others. Every voice matters, so every ear matters, too. Thank you!" What should we do because we have the right to play? Share the ball and take turns. Why does every ear matter? Because every voice matters. The audience claps, and Olive rings her bell. Then the Tree of Voices begins to glow. A third golden leaf slowly grows on its branch! Now, phonics. Let's review. Do you like that one? No, I like THIS one. Interview. Inter means each other, so you see each other and talk. Coexist. Co means together, so coexist means live together. Security. Secure, drop the e, and add ity. Say it strongly, se-CU-ri-ty. Next time, a very special visitor from the town is coming to the Hall of Wisdom!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, We have the right to speak, and we should listen to others. And the third golden leaf is shining on the Tree of Voices! This morning, a special guest walks into the round meeting hall. She has a big smile and a red scarf. It's Mayor Hart, the mayor of Willowford! She shakes hands with everyone and gives Olive a letter. Let's read Mayor Hart's letter. "Dear Children's Council, I am happy to inform you that the town of Willowford would like to receive your ideas. Children see things that adults sometimes miss. We request your help with one question: How can we make Willowford better? Please share your suggestions with me next week. Every good idea is welcome, big or small. With warm wishes, Mayor Hart." What does Mayor Hart want to know? How we can make Willowford better. When should the council share their ideas? Next week. Kiko thinks about the station. It's a little gray and plain. She raises her hand and says, I suggest that we plant flowers at the station. Say it with me. I suggest that we plant flowers at the station. Lovely! The words I suggest that we are polite and a little formal. After it, just put the verb: I suggest that we plant, I suggest that we clean. With friends, you can also say, How about planting flowers? or Why don't we plant flowers? Haru says, That's a good idea, but who will water them? Riko answers, Why don't we ask the station staff to help? Now, phonics. In letters and notices, we often use formal words. Kids becomes children. Get becomes receive. Remember, after c, write e before i: r, e, c, e, i, v, e. Ask for becomes request. Both kinds of words are correct English. Next time, we will share even more ideas for Willowford!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, I suggest that we plant flowers at the station. Today, the Children's Council has a brainstorm. In a brainstorm, everyone shares lots of ideas, and nobody says, That's a bad idea. Olive gives everyone sticky notes. Write one idea on each note, and stick it on the idea board! Leo writes, A new soccer goal. Amara writes, A bird house in the park. Then Priya says, When my teacher and I arrived at Willowford Station, we couldn't find the Hall of Wisdom. We got a little lost. How about making a map for visitors? Say it with me. How about making a map for visitors? Fantastic! Let's read the idea board. "Our Idea Board. Flowers at the station. A new bench by the pond. A bird house in the park. A map for visitors with the library, the park, the Hall of Wisdom, and the best places to eat. The town could provide free maps at the station. Shops could assist by giving maps to visitors, too. We could draw the pictures ourselves, so we don't need to purchase anything expensive." Where could the town give out free maps? At the station. Who could draw the pictures? The children. Then the friends talk about the map. Kiko says, I think a paper map is better because everyone can use it. Haru partly agrees. He says, A big map board outside the station is good, too, because many people can look at it together. Now, phonics. Here are three more formal words. Buy becomes purchase. It ends with a, s, e. Help becomes assist. Assist has two s's in the middle. Give becomes provide. You often see these words on signs and notices. Next time, Leo and Amara want to use the same empty lot for two different things. What will they do?

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, How about making a map for visitors? Today, Olive takes us outside, with Ms. Emma, to the empty lot next to the Hall of Wisdom. It's just dirt and a few old stones now, and the old fence needs to be repaired. Mayor Hart wants to know what the children would like here. Leo says, I think it should be a playground, because children need a place to run and play. Amara says, I see your point, but I think it should be a flower garden. Flowers make people happy, and bees need them, too. Leo and Amara are both right, so what can we do? Olive says, When two people want different things, we can look for a compromise（だきょうあん）. A compromise is an idea where both sides get some of what they want. Let's find a compromise. Say it with me. Let's find a compromise. Great job! Let's read Olive's notes on the board. "The Empty Lot. Leo's idea: a playground. Good points: children can run, climb, and play together. Amara's idea: a flower garden. Good points: it is beautiful, quiet, and good for bees. Our compromise: perhaps we can use both halves of the lot. A flower garden on one side and a small playground on the other side. It will require some benches and a path in the middle, so families can enjoy both." What is good about a flower garden? It is beautiful, quiet, and good for bees. What will be in the middle? Some benches and a path. Kiko says, What if we make a flower garden with a small playground? Leo and Amara smile. That sounds fair! Now, phonics. Maybe becomes perhaps. Need becomes require. R, e, q, u, i, r, e. Fix becomes repair. These formal words are common on notices. Next time, the council will vote on which idea to present to Mayor Hart!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, Let's find a compromise. Leo and Amara were so happy with the garden and the small playground. Now, the council has many ideas, but Mayor Hart is coming back tomorrow, and we can present only one proposal. How can we choose fairly? Olive says, Let's vote! There are twenty children on the council. Each child writes one idea on a card and puts it in the ballot box. Then Riko and Leo count the votes, and Kiko writes the results on the board. Let's read the results. "Children's Council Vote Results. Twenty children voted today. The visitor map got twelve votes. The flowers at the station got five votes. A new bench by the pond got three votes. Twelve out of twenty is more than half, so the majority voted for the visitor map. We will present the map idea to Mayor Hart tomorrow. Thank you, everyone, for sharing your ideas and voting kindly." How many votes did the bench get? Three. Did the majority vote for the map? Yes, because twelve out of twenty is more than half. Haru reports the result. Twelve people voted for the idea. Say it with me. Twelve people voted for the idea. Perfect! Kiko voted for the flowers. She says, I'm a little sad, but the map is a great idea, too. Olive says, Thank you, Kiko. Accepting the result is a big part of voting. And perhaps the flowers can be our next idea! Now, phonics. More formal words. Tell becomes inform. Bike becomes bicycle. Bi means two, and cycle means wheel, so a bicycle has two wheels. Photo becomes photograph. P, h makes the f sound. Next time, we will present our proposal to Mayor Hart in the great hall!

phonics.tipJa: ふりかえり。receive（get の かしこまった ことば。c の あとは ei）、I said THURSDAY（Tuesday? と きかれたら THURSDAY を つよく）、interact（inter ＝ おたがいに ＋ act → かかわりあう）、reality（real ＋ ity → ほんとうの こと。AL を つよく: re-AL-i-ty）。

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, Twelve people voted for the idea. Today is the big day. Mayor Hart sits in the round meeting hall, with her big smile and her red scarf. The Children's Council is ready. We worked on the map all week. Amara drew the pictures, Leo checked the walking times, and Priya wrote the words. Haru, Riko, Kiko, and Birimo walk to the podium. Haru begins. Our proposal is to make a map for visitors. It will help people find their way. Say it with me. Our proposal is to make a map for visitors. It will help people find their way. Excellent! Let's read our proposal. "The Children's Proposal for Willowford. Many visitors get lost when they arrive at Willowford Station. Our proposal is to make a free map for visitors. It will show the library, the park, the Hall of Wisdom, and the new garden. The map will have pictures, so even small children can read it. We also suggest that the town put a big map board outside the station. Thank you for listening." Why will the map have pictures? So even small children can read it. Where should the big map board go? Outside the station. Mayor Hart asks, Why not use a phone instead? Kiko answers, I see your point, but not everyone has a phone. Mayor Hart laughs and says, That's a very good answer. Yes! We will make your map! Everyone cheers, and the applause is very loud. Then the Tree of Voices glows, and a fourth golden leaf grows! Now, phonics. Let's review. Receive. After c, write e before i. Did you say Tuesday? No, I said THURSDAY. Interact. Inter means each other, so interact means act with each other. Reality. Real plus ity. Next time, Amara has a big question about animals!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, Our proposal is to make a map for visitors. It will help people find their way. Mayor Hart loved our map idea, and four golden leaves are shining on the Tree of Voices. Today's council topic is animals. Amara raises her hand. She says, I saw a baby fox in a video. It was so cute! I want one as a pet! Leo says, Hmm, but a fox is a wild animal. So Olive writes a big question on the board. Should people keep wild animals as pets? Say it with me. Should people keep wild animals as pets? Great! Olive says, Let's listen to both sides before we decide. Let's read the fact card from the Hall's library. "Wild animals usually live in nature, like foxes, owls and monkeys. They need lots of space, special food, and other animals of their own kind. Many places have laws that protect wild animals. Keeping them at home can be bad for the animal and unsafe for people. Dogs, cats, rabbits and hamsters are animals that live well with people. Some wild animals are cared for by experts in zoos and sanctuaries." What do wild animals need? Lots of space, special food, and friends of their kind. Listen. A baby fox is the cutest animal in the world. Is that a fact or an opinion? It's an opinion! Amara thinks and says, I partly agree with Leo. Maybe I can draw foxes and visit them at a sanctuary with my family. Olive says, On the one hand, people love animals. On the other hand, wild animals need lots of space. Now, phonics.Spect means look. In plus spect is inspect. To inspect means to look inside carefully. Dict means say. Pre means before, so predict means to say what will happen before it happens. Struct means build. A structure is something built, like a bridge. Next time, we will talk about using less plastic!

vocab.ja: くりかえし つかえる ボトル・マイボトル

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, Should people keep wild animals as pets? Amara decided to draw foxes instead. Today, at lunchtime, Priya comes into the round hall with a big blue box. It's the recycling bin from the Hall's kitchen. She says, Yesterday, I counted the plastic bottles in this bin. There were thirty-one! Haru says, Wow, in only one day! Olive rings her bell. Let's make a suggestion. Remember, we can say, I suggest that we, and then a verb. Riko raises her hand. I suggest that we bring our own bottles. Say it with me. I suggest that we bring our own bottles. Excellent! Kiko adds, How about using reusable bags, too? Priya made a poster about plastic. Let's read Priya's poster. "Did you know? Plastic is strong and useful, but it can take hundreds of years to break down. A lot of plastic waste ends up in the sea, and it can hurt sea animals like turtles and seabirds. Here are three easy ideas. Bring your own bottle and fill it with water. Carry a reusable bag when you go shopping. Say no, thank you, to straws you don't need. Small steps can make a big difference!" How long can plastic take to break down? Hundreds of years. Which animals can plastic hurt? Sea animals, like turtles and seabirds. Then Haru says, I partly agree. Reusable bottles are great, but sometimes I forget mine. Riko says, I see your point. Why don't we put a bottle sticker on the door to remind us? Now, phonics. More roots! Port means carry. Ex means out, so export means to carry things out to another country. Rupt means break. Inter means between, so interrupt means to break in when someone is talking. Ject means throw. Re means back, so reject means to throw something back, or to say no to it. Next time, we will review how we share opinions!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, I suggest that we bring our own bottles. This morning, almost everyone came with their own bottle! Ms. Emma says, Stage 4 is almost over. Let's look back at how we share opinions. In Stage 4, we learned to give an opinion with a reason and an example. We also learned to disagree politely. Olive says, Good listeners make good speakers. Then she starts Opinion Ping-Pong. One person shares an opinion, and the next answers kindly. Birimo jumps up and says, I'm playing a boy who wants a pet monkey! A monkey can live in my room! Kiko answers, I see your point, but I think wild animals should live in nature. Say it with me. I see your point, but I think wild animals should live in nature. Perfect! Birimo asks, What do you mean by nature? Kiko says, I mean forests, rivers and the sea. Haru adds, I think so, too. For example, a monkey needs tall trees and its family. Let's read Olive's card for good speakers. "How to Share an Opinion. First, say your opinion with I think or In my opinion. Next, give a reason with because. Then, add an example with For example. When you disagree, be kind and say, I see your point, but. When you don't understand, ask, What do you mean by this word? Listen to the end and don't interrupt. Remember, we can disagree and still be good friends." Which word do we use to give a reason? Because. What should we do when we disagree? Be kind. Birimo laughs. OK, no monkey. Maybe a hamster! Now, phonics. Spect means look, and re means again. When you respect someone, you look at them with kind eyes. Dict means say, and contra means against. To contradict means to say the opposite. Struct means build, and con means together. To construct means to build. Next time, we will explain a graph about plastic!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, I see your point, but I think wild animals should live in nature. Today, we review explaining graphs and places. For two months, Kiko and Riko counted the plastic bottles in the recycling bin every day. Now they show a bar graph on the big screen with a projector. Riko points to the bars and says, This tall bar is last month. This short bar is this month. The graph shows that our class used less plastic this month. Say it with me. The graph shows that our class used less plastic this month. Wonderful! Kiko adds, It went down from one hundred twenty to forty. Leo says, That's a big difference! Let's read the report under the graph. "Plastic Bottles at the Hall of Wisdom. Last month, the Children's Council used one hundred twenty plastic bottles. This month, we used only forty. That is two thirds less! Most members now bring their own bottles. The recycling bin is next to the kitchen door, and the water fountain is to the right of the stairs, so please fill your bottle there. Let's keep going and make the next bar even shorter!" How many bottles did the council use this month? Forty. Where is the water fountain? To the right of the stairs. Then Haru says, I think the bottle sticker on the door helped the most, because we see it every morning. Riko says, I partly agree, but Priya's poster helped, too. For example, Amara read it and stopped buying bottles. Now, phonics. Port means carry, and trans means across. To transport means to carry people or things from one place to another. Rupt means break. E means out, so when a volcano erupts, hot lava breaks out. Ject means throw, and pro means forward. When we project a picture, we throw it forward onto a screen. Next time, we will get ready for the big council meeting with polite requests!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, The graph shows that our class used less plastic this month. Soon, children from many places will come for the big council meeting. Olive says, We need forty folding chairs in a circle. Let's get ready together. Ms. Emma says, Let's review polite requests. Haru sees Leo and asks, Would you mind helping us set up the chairs? Say it with me. Would you mind helping us set up the chairs? Great! Leo says, Not at all! Remember, Not at all means, Sure, I'm happy to help. Then Riko asks Ms. Emma, Could you put a name card on each chair? Ms. Emma says, Sure, no problem. Let's read Olive's checklist. "Big Council Meeting Checklist. Put forty folding chairs in a big circle. Place a name card on each chair. Fill the water jugs and put them on the side table. Hang the welcome banner over the main door with an adult. Keep the aisles clear so that everyone can walk safely. Take a break when you feel tired, and drink some water. When everything is ready, we will meet at four o'clock by the Tree of Voices." How many chairs do we need? Forty. When will we meet? At four o'clock. Then Birimo climbs onto a chair to hang the banner. Ms. Emma says, Birimo, would you mind not standing on the chair? Let's ask an adult with a ladder. Birimo says, Oh, sorry! Good idea. Kiko says, I think this was our best teamwork, because everyone helped. Riko says, I agree. Suddenly, a fifth golden leaf grows on the Tree of Voices! Now, phonics. Let's review. Export means to carry things out to other countries. Ject means throw, so reject means to throw back, or to say no. Purchase is the formal word for buy. It ends in a, s, e. Should we meet at three? No, let's meet at FOUR. Next time, we will read two opinions about homework!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, Would you mind helping us set up the chairs? The chairs are ready, and the fifth golden leaf is shining. Today, Olive gives us the Children's Council newsletter. Inside, there are two short opinion pieces about homework. One is by Leo, and one is by Priya. Ms. Emma says, Let's think like a judge and check the reasons. Read two opinions. Which do you agree with? Say it with me. Read two opinions. Which do you agree with? Nice! Let's read the two opinion pieces. "Leo writes, I think we should have homework every day. When we practice a little every day, we remember more. For example, I learned my times tables with ten minutes of homework a day. Priya writes, I think some days without homework are a good idea. Children need time to read, play and rest. For example, on free evenings, I read science books and go to bed early." What does Leo think? We should have homework every day. What does Priya do on free evenings? She reads science books and goes to bed early. Leo learned his times tables with ten minutes of homework a day. Is that a fact or an opinion? It's a fact. It really happened. Some days without homework are a good idea. That one is an opinion. Haru says, I agree with Leo because practice helps us remember. Riko says, I see your point, but rest is important, too. Kiko says, Both writers give good reasons. Maybe the best answer is somewhere in the middle, like short homework on most days and some free days. Now, phonics. Let's review. Popularity is popular plus ity. The internet has inter, which means between, because computers connect with each other. Do you feed the cat? No, I feed the DOG. Require is the formal word for need. Respect has spect, which means look. Next time, we will write a proposal letter to Mayor Hart!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, Read two opinions. Which do you agree with? Mayor Hart sent us a note. It says, Thank you for the visitor map! Please send me more ideas in a letter. Leo says, Yesterday, our group walked through Willowford Park with the adults. Many grandparents and parents with babies wanted to sit down, but there were only two benches. So we write a proposal letter. It starts with Dear. Dear Mayor, I suggest that we put more benches in the park. Say it with me. Dear Mayor, I suggest that we put more benches in the park. Lovely! Kiko asks, Do I write my address? Ms. Emma says, No, you don't need to. Just sign it, The Children's Council. Before we write, Riko says, I think the benches should go near the playground, because parents watch their children there. Haru says, I partly agree, but under the trees is cooler in summer. So we choose both! Let's read our letter. "Dear Mayor Hart, Thank you for listening to children. I suggest that we put more benches in Willowford Park. Right now, there are only two benches, so many visitors have to stand. Benches would help grandparents, parents with babies, and anyone who feels tired. We think four new benches would be enough, two near the playground and two under the big trees. I look forward to hearing from you. Best wishes, The Children's Council." How many benches are in the park now? Only two. Where should the new benches go? Two near the playground and two under the big trees. Now, phonics. Let's review. Activity is active, drop the e, plus ity. A coworker works together with you, because co means together. Does Haru feed the fish? No, KIKO feeds the fish. Request is the formal way to say ask for. Contradict has dict, which means say, so it means to say the opposite. Next time, we will practice for a friendly debate!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, Dear Mayor, I suggest that we put more benches in the park. Today, we are practicing for the big council meeting, because there will be a friendly debate. The question is, Should every school have a school garden? In a debate, one team says yes, and the other team says no. Sometimes you speak for a side you don't agree with. That helps us understand others. Haru and Kiko are on the Yes team. Riko and Birimo are on the No team. Olive sets a timer for one minute. Haru stands up and begins. First, I'd like to say that school gardens teach us about nature. Say it with me. First, I'd like to say that school gardens teach us about nature. Excellent! Let's read the notes from both teams. "Yes Team. School gardens teach us where our food comes from. Children can grow vegetables and flowers, and the flowers help bees. No Team. Gardens need a lot of time and water. Someone has to take care of the plants in the summer holidays. Some schools are very small and have no space, so a garden might be difficult. A plant box in each classroom could be another idea." What do the flowers in a school garden help? Bees. What is one problem in the holidays? Someone has to take care of the plants. Riko says, That's true, but who will water the plants in the holidays? Kiko answers, I see your point. Maybe families can take turns. At the end, Ms. Emma says, To sum up, both teams made good points. Everyone shakes hands. Now, phonics. Let's review. Ability comes from able. Ble changes to bil. An intersection is where roads cross, and inter means between. Do you wash the dishes? No, I DRY the dishes. Inform is the formal word for tell. Construct has struct, which means build. Next time, we will look back at our days at the Hall!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, First, I'd like to say that school gardens teach us about nature. Tomorrow is the big council meeting, and then we will say goodbye to the Hall of Wisdom. Today, we sit under the Tree of Voices and look back at our time here. Kiko feels two things at once. She says, On the one hand, I'm sad to leave. On the other hand, I'm excited about our next adventure. Say it with me. On the one hand, I'm sad to leave. On the other hand, I'm excited about our next adventure. Beautiful! Let's read Olive's memory board. "Our Days at the Hall of Wisdom. We talked about school rules and listened to both sides. We learned to be fair, to stand up for a friend, and to invite everyone to play. We learned about children's rights and our responsibilities. We made a visitor map for Willowford, wrote a letter to Mayor Hart, and used less plastic. Most of all, we learned that good listeners make good speakers." What did we make for Willowford? A visitor map. What did we learn most of all? Good listeners make good speakers. Then Birimo goes to return a book to the Hall's library with Ms. Emma. On the top bookshelf, he sees a very old map. Ms. Emma reaches up and takes it down for him. The map shows a path that goes down, down, down to the bottom of the sea. At the end, there is a tiny picture of shining domes and the words Deep Sea City. Birimo whispers, Wow! Now, phonics. Let's review. Curiosity comes from curious. Ous changes to os, then add ity. Birimo is full of curiosity! A costar is a star in a movie together with another star. Do you clean on Sunday? No, we clean on SATURDAY. Provide is the formal word for give. Transport means to carry across. Next time, it's our grand finale!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, On the one hand, I'm sad to leave. On the other hand, I'm excited about our next adventure. The great hall is full. Children from many places sit in a big circle, and Mayor Hart sits with them in her red scarf. Olive rings her little bell. Ding! Welcome to the Children's Council! Every voice matters! First comes the school garden debate. Then Riko shows the bar graph about plastic, and Haru reads our letter about benches. Mayor Hart says, Good news! Willowford Park will get four new benches! At the end, the whole council writes one message together, and Kiko reads it aloud. Children's voices can change the world. Say it with me. Children's voices can change the world. Wonderful! Let's read the message of the Children's Council. "The Message of the Children's Council. We come from mountain towns, seaside villages and big cities, but we all have something to say. We share our ideas kindly. We listen to the end, even when we disagree. We look at both sides and find a compromise. We take care of our town, our animals and our sea. We believe that children's voices can change the world." Where do the children come from? Mountain towns, seaside villages and big cities. What do we take care of? Our town, our animals and our sea. Then something magical happens. A sixth golden leaf grows, and the Tree of Voices blooms with white flowers! Olive gives each of us a tiny wooden bell. She says, Ring it whenever you want to share an idea. Now, phonics. Let's review. Equality means being equal. International means between nations. Do you like that one? No, I like THIS one. Children is the formal word for kids. Interrupt means to break in, so please don't interrupt. Suddenly, Birimo's old sea map glows blue. Our next adventure is under the sea! Goodbye, Olive! Thank you, Hall of Wisdom!
